items.title: Mendeleev predicted germanium 15 years before anyone made it
items.claim: In 1871 Mendeleev published predicted properties for an undiscovered element he called 'eka-silicon'. In 1886 Winkler isolated germanium. The predicted atomic mass was 72; measured 72.6. Predicted density 5.5 g/cm3; measured 5.32.
items.prompt: How could Mendeleev predict an unknown element?

options.text: He used patterns in the existing table: rows and columns of known elements bracketed each gap. An element in the silicon column, between gallium and arsenic, must have intermediate properties — and atomic mass close to the average of its neighbours
He had advance information from chemists in Germany

items.reveal:
Mendeleev's 1871 predicted properties for eka-silicon: atomic mass ~72, density ~5.5 g/cm3, grey metal, oxide formula MO2 with density ~4.7 g/cm3, chloride MCl4 boiling under 100°C.

Winkler's 1886 germanium: atomic mass 72.6, density 5.32 g/cm3, grey metal, GeO2 density 4.7 g/cm3, GeCl4 boiling at 86°C.

The match converted scepticism into acceptance. The periodic table stopped being a memorisation aid and became a predictive theory. Similar predictions held for gallium (eka-aluminium, 1875) and scandium (eka-boron, 1879).

The predictions could not have worked if the table were merely an empirical classification. The fact that it predicted real properties of unknown elements showed that something deeper was being captured.
items.why: Theories earn their keep by predicting what no one has measured yet. Mendeleev's table did this three times in 17 years.

items.title: The 'inert' gases are not entirely inert
items.claim: Argon, krypton, xenon and radon all form chemical compounds. XeF2, XeF4 and XeF6 are stable solids that can be bought from chemical suppliers. The textbook claim that noble gases 'don't react' is a simplification.
items.prompt: Why can xenon — but not helium or neon — form compounds?

options.text: Xenon has a different number of valence electrons

Xenon's outer electrons are far from the nucleus and weakly held (low ionisation energy, 1170 kJ/mol); the strongest oxidisers like PtF6 and F2 can strip or share them. Helium and neon hold their electrons too tightly
Xenon contains a hidden valence electron

items.reveal:
Until 1962, every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at the University of British Columbia noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) is essentially the same as xenon's (1170 kJ/mol). He had just shown PtF6 could oxidise O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.

XeF2 is now made by simply mixing Xe and F2 in sunlight. XeF4 forms colourless crystals. XeO3 is a powerful explosive. Krypton compounds (KrF2) exist at low temperature. Even argon was forced to form HArF in 2000.

Helium and neon, the lightest noble gases, have ionisation energies around 2080 and 2370 kJ/mol — too high to be broken even by the strongest oxidisers in normal conditions.
items.why: 'Inert' is a useful summary, not a law of nature. Strong enough chemistry breaks even the rule of full octets.

items.title: Fireworks colours are atomic fingerprints
items.claim: Lithium gives a red flame. Sodium gives orange. Potassium lilac. Copper blue-green. Strontium crimson. Each element produces a characteristic colour because electrons fall through fixed energy gaps.

options.text: Heating excites electrons; they fall back to lower energy levels, emitting photons of specific wavelengths set by the spacing of the atom's electron energy levels — colour is set by the element, not the flame
The shape of the metal sample
The amount of oxygen in the flame

items.reveal_title: Spectra are the unique signatures of atoms
items.reveal:
Each element has its own set of allowed electron energy levels — set by the quantum mechanics of its electrons and nucleus. A flame thermally excites electrons; as they relax, photons emerge with energies exactly equal to the gap between levels (E = hf).

Sodium's strong 'D line' at 589 nm (orange) is the 3p-to-3s transition. The bright yellow streetlights you see are sodium-vapour lamps using the same transition.

This is also how astronomers identify elements in stars they can never visit: they fit the dark or bright lines in stellar spectra to known atomic transition wavelengths. Helium was discovered in the Sun (1868) before being found on Earth (1895) using exactly this technique.
items.why: Flame colours look like a simple party trick. They are direct measurements of quantum-mechanical energy levels.
